deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from the preceding pages): q = 2p+1 is prime. The quadratic residues are the least positive remainders of 1^2, 2^2, ..., p^2 mod q. There are p of them: 1, alpha, beta, gamma, .... The other p numbers below q are the non-residues A, B, C, ... (Fraktur in the manuscript). This page builds the multiplicative structure of the two classes.

(End of section 298) Section 297 showed that the powers 1, m, m^2, ... of a residue m stay among the residues. Section 298 concludes that some power m^j with j <= p must be congruent to 1. [Mine: by pigeonhole, the p+1 powers m^0, ..., m^p fall into only p residue classes, so m^i ≡ m^j for some i<j, hence m^(j-i) ≡ 1.] Euler adds that m^p ≡ 1 directly: if m = a^2 - k q, then m^p ≡ a^(2p) = a^(q-1) ≡ 1 mod q. This is Fermat's little theorem, proved earlier in the treatise. It is the necessity half of Euler's criterion.

Section 299 (quotient of residues is a residue). Suppose m ≡ a^2 and mn ≡ b^2 (mod q), with gcd(a,q) = gcd(b,q) = 1. Then n a^2 ≡ mn ≡ b^2, so q divides b^2 - n a^2.

Section 300. Since q | b^2 - n a^2, also q | (b + kq)^2 - n a^2 for every integer k. Because gcd(a,q) = 1, one can choose k with b + kq = a c, that is, kq ≡ -b (mod a). Then q | a^2 c^2 - n a^2 = a^2 (c^2 - n). Since q is prime and does not divide a [mine], q | c^2 - n. So n ≡ c^2 is a residue. This is division mod q done without explicit inverses (c ≡ b a^(-1)).

Section 301. If alpha is a residue and A a non-residue, then alpha·A is a non-residue. Otherwise, by 299 applied to alpha and alpha·A, A would be a residue.

Section 302. If mn is a residue and m is a non-residue, then n is a non-residue. Otherwise, by 299, m would be a residue.

Section 303. Claim: the product of two non-residues is a residue. Squares A^2, B^2 are obviously residues; the general product AB needs proof.

Section 304. Fix one non-residue A. The numbers A, alpha·A, beta·A, ... (reduced mod q) are p numbers. They are pairwise distinct [mine: alpha A ≡ beta A implies q | (alpha - beta) A, hence alpha ≡ beta]. By 301 they are all non-residues. Since there are exactly p non-residues, these are all of them: the non-residues form the coset A·R of the residue group R.

Sections 305-306. Any two non-residues can be written D = delta·A and E = epsilon·A with delta, epsilon residues. Then DE = (delta·epsilon)·A^2. Here delta·epsilon is a residue (by 293), and A^2 is a square, hence a residue. So DE is a residue.

Section 307. Summary:
- R·R = R
- R·N = N
- N·N = R

In modern terms, the Legendre symbol is multiplicative, and the residues form an index-2 subgroup of (Z/qZ)^*.
errors: Section 300: Euler says k should be chosen so that k(2p+1) divided by a 'leaves b'. For b + k(2p+1) = ac one needs k(2p+1) ≡ -b (mod a), i.e. remainder a - b (or 'falls short of a multiple of a by b'). This is a minor sign/wording slip; the existence claim is correct because gcd(a, 2p+1) = 1.

Section 300: the cancellation of a^2 from q | a^2(c^2 - n) uses that the prime q does not divide a. This is stated earlier ('existentibus a et b ad 2p+1 primis') but not invoked explicitly at this step. Not an error.
Section 304: the distinctness of alpha·A, beta·A, ... is asserted without proof. It is true because q is prime and A is coprime to q.
Section 298: 'manifesto' relies on Fermat's little theorem a^(2p) ≡ 1, established earlier in the treatise. Not an error.

results.what: If m is a quadratic residue mod prime 2p+1 then m^p ≡ 1 (mod 2p+1)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (1750s, e.g. E262/E242 and this Tractatus)

results.what: If m and mn are residues then n is a residue (proof via choosing c with ac ≡ b)
results.modern_name: Quadratic residues form a subgroup of (Z/pZ)^* (closure under quotients)

results.what: Residue × non-residue = non-residue; non-residues form the coset A·R; non-residue × non-residue = residue
results.modern_name: Multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol / index-2 subgroup of squares
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, c.1750; also Theoremata circa residua E262), later formalized by Legendre and Gauss

deep.surprise_reason: This is the standard, well-known content of Euler's Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, Ch. 10 (published 1849). The multiplicative rules for residues and non-residues and the half of Euler's criterion are classically attributed to Euler. The coset argument in 304-306 is elegant but known.

checkable.sympy: all(pow(m, (q-1)//2, q) == 1 for q in [3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23,29] for m in set(x**2 % q for x in range(1, q)))
checkable.asserts: Section 298: every quadratic residue m mod prime q=2p+1 satisfies m^p ≡ 1

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(a*b % q, q) == legendre_symbol(a, q)*legendre_symbol(b, q) for q in [3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23,29] for a in range(1, q) for b in range(1, q))
checkable.asserts: Section 307: RR=R, RN=N, NN=R (multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol)

checkable.sympy: (lambda q, A: sorted(set((r*A) % q for r in set(x**2 % q for x in range(1, q)))) == sorted(set(range(1, q)) - set(x**2 % q for x in range(1, q))))(23, 5)
checkable.asserts: Section 304: for q=23 and non-residue A=5, {alpha*A mod q : alpha a residue} is exactly the set of non-residues
